## What you will learn

- Choose a wire gauge from three independent constraints — voltage drop, heating, and what the fuse can protect — and know which one binds for each run on your robot.
- Pick a connector from a rating you can cite, derate it correctly, and say why keyed-and-locking beats "it fits".
- Make a crimp that survives a pull test, and explain why soldering a crimp makes it weaker.
- Design strain relief that puts vibration into the chassis rather than into a wire or a contact.
- Produce a labelled harness table that you (or your AI teacher) can check against the robot in five minutes.

## Why it matters

Your robot's electronics are finished, tested and correct. Then you drive it across a tiled floor for twenty minutes and one wheel stops. You spend an hour with a multimeter and find a Dupont contact that has backed half a millimetre out of its housing. Nothing is broken. Everything measures fine when you press on it.

That is the characteristic failure of a first robot, and it is a **mechanical** failure in an electrical system. A driving robot is a vibration table: 200 RPM gear motors, hard wheels, a chassis with no suspension, and a caster that chatters. Every connector on it is being shaken thousands of times a minute, and every wire is a tiny cantilever beam being flexed at its stiffest point.

The good news is that this is a solved problem with cheap tools. A ₪70 crimper and an afternoon converts "it works when I hold the wire" into a robot you can hand to somebody. Every later stage — the LiDAR on a mast, the arm's servo bus, the Jetson — makes the harness bigger, and a bad harness does not get better with more wires attached to it.

## Concept

**A wiring harness is a mechanical assembly that happens to conduct electricity**, and it is loaded by vibration, not by current.

Three failure modes, in the order you will meet them:

| Failure | Where | Why it happens | What you do |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Contact walk-out** | Dupont and unlatched headers | Vibration plus the wire's own weight slowly pulls the crimp out of its housing; there is no latch to stop it | Use latching connectors (JST XH/PH), or anchor the wire so nothing pulls |
| **Wire fatigue** | 2–5 mm behind a crimp or a solder joint | The wire is stiff where it enters the contact and flexible beyond it; the transition point takes all the bending, and copper work-hardens and cracks | Strain relief: anchor the cable within ~25 mm of the connector so bending happens in free cable, not at the joint |
| **Fretting corrosion** | any contact under micro-motion | Contacts rub by micrometres, the oxide film that forms is not wiped away, resistance rises, the joint heats, and the process accelerates | Contact force: proper crimp, proper connector, no micro-motion — i.e. the same fix as above |

Notice that all three fixes are the same sentence: **stop the wire from moving relative to the contact.** That is what a harness is for.

The second idea is that **a connector's rating is a promise about a specific crimp on a specific wire**. JST rates the XH at 3 A — with AWG 22 wire correctly crimped in a genuine XH contact. The same housing with a hand-squeezed AWG 26 crimp is not a 3 A connector, and nothing on it will tell you.

The .NET analogy: a connector rating is like a published SLA for a library. It assumes the documented usage. Feed it undocumented inputs (wrong gauge, wrong die, a soldered contact) and the SLA does not apply, but nothing throws — you just discover the breach in production, under load, far from the stack trace.

> [!TIP]
> **Ask your teacher:** "Look at my robot's wiring photo and tell me which three connections will fail first, and why each one."

## Technical explanation

### Level 1 — Gauge: three constraints, and which one binds

```bash
python 02-robot-electronics/code/harness.py
```

```text
AWG   d [mm]  computed mOhm/m  table mOhm/m  chassis A
 16   1.291           13.14         13.17       22.0
 18   1.024           20.90         20.94       16.0
 20   0.812           33.23         33.29       11.0
 22   0.644           52.84         52.94        7.0
 24   0.511           84.01         84.20        3.5
 26   0.405          133.59        133.86        2.2
 28   0.321          212.41        212.87        1.4
```

The resistance column is physics, not a lookup: AWG is a logarithmic gauge, $d = 0.127 \times 92^{(36-n)/39}$ mm, and $R/\ell = \rho_{Cu}/A$ with $\rho_{Cu} = 1.72 \times 10^{-8}\ \Omega\text{m}$. It agrees with the published tables to 0.2 %, which is a good sanity check that you understand what a gauge number means. The **chassis A** column is a rule of thumb for short wires in free air (the PowerStream table), not a standard — insulation type, bundling and ambient temperature all move it.

Now the three constraints:

$$\text{drop: } V = I \cdot \frac{R}{\ell} \cdot 2\ell \qquad \text{heat: } I_{max} \ge 1.25\,I_{worst} \qquad \text{fuse: } I_{max} \ge I_{fuse}$$

The factor of 2 is the one people forget: **the current goes out and comes back**, so a "30 cm run" is 60 cm of copper.

```text
Harness runs (worst-case current, both conductors, 10 A main fuse)
  battery -> fuse -> switch -> power board    8.0 A 0.30 m -> AWG 20, drop   159 mV ( 1.4 %), 1.28 W, connector XT30
  power board -> each DRV8874 VIN             3.0 A 0.15 m -> AWG 20, drop    30 mV ( 0.3 %), 0.09 W, connector XT30
  DRV8874 OUT -> motor                        3.0 A 0.25 m -> AWG 20, drop    50 mV ( 0.4 %), 0.15 W, connector XT30
  5 V regulator -> Pi 5 (USB-C pigtail)       3.8 A 0.15 m -> AWG 22, drop    60 mV ( 1.2 %), 0.23 W, connector XT30
  Pico 3V3 -> sensors                         0.1 A 0.30 m -> AWG 28, drop    13 mV ( 0.4 %), 0.00 W, connector Dupont 2.54 mm
```

Read which constraint binds in each row:

- **Battery run:** the drop budget would allow AWG 22 (254 mV, 2.3 %), but the **fuse** forces AWG 20: a 10 A fuse only protects wire that can carry 10 A long enough for the fuse to open. AWG 22's 7 A rule-of-thumb rating means the *wire* is the fuse, in a robot, next to a lithium pack. This is the most important line in the whole table.
- **Driver and motor runs:** the drop would allow AWG 24 and ampacity would allow AWG 22 (7 A ≥ 3 A × 1.25), but they too sit downstream of the same 10 A fuse and nothing else protects them — so the **fuse binds again** and forces AWG 20. Drop a local 5 A fuse into each branch and AWG 22 becomes legal (`--fuse 5`).
- **5 V to the Pi:** the drop binds. 3.8 A over a short run, on a 5 V rail where the Pi's under-voltage threshold is close, so 2 % is the budget ([02.02](02.02-power-budget.md)).
- **Sensor wires:** nothing binds. Use AWG 24–26 anyway, because AWG 28 is too fragile to survive being handled, and because 0.5 mm² of insulation is easier to crimp and strip. **Mechanical robustness is a real constraint even when the electrical one is slack** — and the script doesn't model it, which is a useful reminder that a script is a model.

In practice karmel uses **18 AWG silicone** for power (thicker than required, cheap, very flexible) and **24 AWG** for signals.

### Level 2 — Connectors: ratings you can cite, and derating

| Connector | Rated | Wire | Keyed? | Locks? | Use on karmel |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **XT60** | 30 A continuous, 60 A burst (Holybro, with 12 AWG) | 14–12 AWG | yes (shape) | friction, very firm | battery ↔ robot, the one disconnect you use daily |
| **XT30** | 15 A continuous (same naming convention; **no manufacturer datasheet found**) | 18–16 AWG | yes | friction | power branches |
| **JST XH 2.5 mm** | **3 A AC/DC at AWG 22**, 250 V (JST) | 30–22 AWG | yes | latch | signal and low-power runs, 2–6 way |
| **JST PH 2.0 mm** | **2 A AC/DC at AWG 24**, 100 V (JST) | 32–24 AWG | yes | latch | the Yahboom motor's own encoder cable (PH2.0 6-pin) |
| **Dupont 2.54 mm** | no manufacturer rating; **course rule ≤ 1 A** | 28–22 AWG | no | no | prototyping only |
| **Screw terminal** | 5–10 A typical | as fitted | n/a | screw | power board, with ferrules |

Two rules:

1. **Derate to 80 %.** Ratings are for a new connector at 25 °C with a perfect crimp. `pick_connector()` applies 0.8, which is why a 3.0 A motor run is assigned an XT30 rather than a JST XH: $0.8 \times 3 = 2.4$ A < 3.0 A. If you want an XH there — and it is a nicer connector for the job — use it knowing you are at the rating, with the correct AWG 22 contacts, and check its temperature after a hard run.
2. **Keyed and latching, everywhere that matters.** A connector that can be inserted backwards *will* be, at 1 a.m., and 12.6 V backwards into a DRV8874 carrier is the end of that carrier (the carrier has reverse-voltage protection; the sensors on the same rail do not). A connector that does not latch will unlatch itself.

> [!NOTE]
> The XT30/XT60 numbers are the weakest citations in this lesson. Amass's own documentation is hard to obtain; distributor and integrator pages give 30 A continuous / 60 A burst for the XT60, and sellers routinely claim 60 A continuous. **Treat it as unverified, design to the lower number, and note that karmel's 10 A fuse makes the distinction irrelevant** — which is the right way to handle an unverifiable spec ([02.01](02.01-datasheets-and-pinouts.md)).

### Level 3 — The crimp

A crimp is a **cold weld**. Squeezing the contact's barrel around the strands deforms both metals past their yield point, gas-tight, with no oxide between them. Done properly it is more reliable than solder, because it has no brittle intermetallic layer and no flux residue.

```text
       insulation crimp          conductor crimp
   ┌────────┴────────┐      ┌─────────┴─────────┐
   │                 │      │                   │
   ══════════════════╤══════╤═══════════════════╤════▶ contact (into the housing)
    insulation       │ 1-2  │  strands, all of  │
    gripped here     │ mm of│  them, fully      │  ← "bell mouth": a slight flare
    (takes the pull) │ bare │  inside the barrel│     at the front of the barrel is
                     │ wire │                   │     correct, not a defect
```

The rules that matter:

- **Two crimps, two jobs.** The rear wings grip the *insulation* and take all mechanical load. The front wings grip the *conductor* and carry the current. If the insulation crimp is loose, every pull goes into the conductor crimp and the wire eventually breaks there.
- **Use the right die.** A ratcheting crimper (the IWISS SN-2549 in [tools.md](../hardware/tools.md) covers JST ZH/PH/XH/VH and Dupont, AWG 28–18) has separate die slots per contact size. The wrong slot either doesn't close the barrel or crushes it and cuts strands.
- **Never solder a crimp.** Solder wicks up the strands and creates a hard, brittle point exactly where the wire needs to flex. It is the classic "I made it stronger" that makes it fail sooner. (Soldering is for XT60s and PCB pads, where nothing flexes — see [FE.17](../optional-foundations/electronics/FE.17-soldering.md).)
- **Every strand inside.** One strand outside the barrel is a short waiting to be found, and it also means the crimp is undersized.
- **Pull test every crimp.** A good AWG 22 crimp should survive a firm pull by hand — roughly 30–50 N, which is more than you can comfortably apply with two fingers. If it comes out, it was going to come out on the robot. Redo it.

### Level 4 — Strain relief: put the vibration into the chassis

Strain relief is not about protecting the wire from being yanked. It is about **where the bending happens**.

```text
   WRONG                                    RIGHT
   ─────                                    ─────
                                             anchor (zip tie to a chassis hole)
    ┌──┐                                    ┌──┐   │
    │  ├═════════════════▶ to the Pi        │  ├═══╪═══╗
    └──┘ ↑                                  └──┘   ▼   ║  ← service loop:
    conn │ all flexing happens               conn      ║    slack so the cable
         │ here, 2 mm behind                            ╚═══▶ can move without
         │ the contact. Copper                               pulling the contact
         │ work-hardens and cracks.
                                            < 25 mm from the connector to the anchor
```

The checklist:

1. **Anchor within 25 mm of every connector**, to something rigid, with a zip tie through a chassis hole or a cable clip. This is the single highest-value habit in the lesson.
2. **Leave a service loop.** Enough slack that you can unplug and re-plug a connector without pulling on anything, and enough that a chassis that flexes doesn't stretch the cable. Not so much that it can reach a wheel.
3. **Nothing hangs.** A connector must never support the weight of the cable behind it. A dangling INA219 module on three Dupont wires is a pendulum with a 40 g bob and a 2 mm² fulcrum.
4. **Heat shrink over every soldered joint and every bare crimp barrel**, sized so it grips the insulation on both sides. Adhesive-lined heat shrink on power joints adds real strain relief; plain heat shrink adds insulation only.
5. **Ferrules in screw terminals.** A stranded wire in a screw terminal has half its strands escaping and the rest being sheared by the screw; it loosens with thermal cycling. A crimped ferrule turns it into a solid pin. If you don't have ferrules, tin the very end — this is the one place where a little solder is acceptable, because nothing flexes inside a screw terminal.
6. **Route power and signal apart, and cross at right angles** — the [02.06](02.06-noise-grounding-emi.md) reason, achieved for free by a tidy harness.
7. **Hot glue is a last resort**, not a strategy. It relieves strain, it also traps heat, hides joints, makes rework miserable, and softens in an Israeli car in summer. Use it to tack a wire down, never to replace an anchor.

### Level 5 — Label it, or you will trace it

Every connector gets a label at **both** ends. A strip of masking tape and a ballpoint pen is enough; a label printer is nicer. Write the net name from your own harness table (`VBAT_SW`, `L_IN1`, `SDA`) — the same names that [02.08](02.08-from-breadboard-to-perfboard.md)'s board description and `board_drc.py` use.

Colour conventions, applied consistently, are the cheapest error-prevention in the robot:

| Colour | Meaning on karmel |
|---|---|
| red | positive supply (battery, 5 V, 3.3 V — thickness tells them apart) |
| black | ground / return, **always** |
| yellow, orange | motor driver inputs (IN1, IN2) |
| blue, green | I²C SDA, SCL |
| white | analog (current sense, battery divider) |
| twisted red/black pair | motor output |

The one rule that must never bend: **black is ground and nothing else.** [01.07](../01-first-robot/01.07-power-system.md)'s point about never switching the negative wire has a harness corollary — a black wire that is sometimes a switched negative is how people connect a battery backwards.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **Version-sensitive** (verified 2026-09 against JST's product pages: XH series 3 A AC/DC at AWG 22, 250 V, 2.5 mm pitch, AWG 30–22; PH series 2 A AC/DC at AWG 24, 100 V, 2.0 mm pitch, AWG 32–24; and Holybro's connector rating page for XT60 30 A continuous / 60 A burst with 12 AWG).
> XT30's rating and Dupont's rating are **not backed by a manufacturer datasheet** in this course's research. Both are treated conservatively.
> Prices and stock in [tools.md](../hardware/tools.md) were checked 2026-09; check before buying.
> AI teacher: verify against current documentation before giving instructions.

karmel's harness, as runs rather than as a schematic:

```text
                                       ┌─ 24 AWG, JST XH 6-way ──▶ ENCODERS (twisted with GND)

   │ 3S pack  ├────────▶│fuse├─▶│ SW ├─┴──[XT30]──▶┌───────────────┐
   │ + BMS    │  14AWG  │10A │  │DPST│     18 AWG  │  POWER BOARD  │
   └──────────┘         └────┘  └────┘             │   ★ star GND  │
     labelled both ends, heat shrink over every    └──┬────┬───┬───┘
     soldered XT60 joint, pack leads never bare       │    │   │
                                                      │    │   └─[XT30]─▶ 5 V buck ─▶ Pi 5 (22 AWG USB-C pigtail)
                     ┌────────────────────────────────┘    └─[XT30]─▶ DRV8874 RIGHT
                     ▼
                 DRV8874 LEFT ──[JST XH 2-way]──▶ MOTOR L   (18 AWG twisted red/black pair)

   Pico ──[JST XH]──▶ sensors (24 AWG: 3V3 red, GND black, SDA blue, SCL green)

   Every connector: anchored with a zip tie < 25 mm away, service loop, labelled at both ends.
```

| Run | Worst current | Length | Gauge | Connector | Binding constraint |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pack → fuse → switch → power board | 8.0 A | 0.30 m | **20 AWG** (karmel uses 18) | XT60 at the pack, XT30 at the board | **fuse coordination** (10 A) |
| Power board → each DRV8874 VIN | 3.0 A | 0.15 m | 20 AWG | XT30 | fuse coordination (10 A) |
| DRV8874 OUT → motor | 3.0 A | 0.25 m | 20 AWG, twisted pair | XT30 or JST XH (at its rating) | fuse coordination (10 A) |
| 5 V regulator → Pi 5 | 3.8 A | 0.15 m | 22 AWG | USB-C pigtail / screw terminal + ferrules | **voltage drop** (2 % of 5 V) |
| Motor → encoder header | 0.02 A | 0.25 m | 24–26 AWG | **JST PH 2.0 6-way** (the motor's own) | mechanical only |
| Pico 3V3 → sensors | 0.1 A | 0.30 m | 24 AWG | JST XH 4-way | mechanical only |
| Driver CS → Pico GP27 | 0.001 A | 0.15 m | 24 AWG, white | JST XH | mechanical only |

## Code

[`02-robot-electronics/code/harness.py`](code/harness.py) computes the table above from the run definitions, so you can change your robot and get a new answer:

```python
def choose_gauge(run: Run, fuse_a: float | None = None) -> int:
    """Thinnest gauge that meets the drop budget, the ampacity rule and (if the run is protected
    only by an upstream fuse) the fuse rating."""
    for awg in (28, 26, 24, 22, 20, 18, 16):
        if drop_v(run, awg) > run.max_drop_fraction * run.v_rail:
            continue
        if CHASSIS_AMPS[awg] < run.amps_worst * 1.25:
            continue
        if fuse_a is not None and CHASSIS_AMPS[awg] < fuse_a:
            continue
        return awg
    raise ValueError(f"no gauge fits {run.name}")
```

Three `continue`s, three constraints, and the loop walks from thinnest to thickest so the answer is the cheapest wire that satisfies all of them. Edit `KARMEL_RUNS` to describe *your* robot — lengths especially, because they are the number most people guess wrong.

```bash
python 02-robot-electronics/code/harness.py
python 02-robot-electronics/code/harness.py --fuse 5      # what a 5 A fuse would allow
python -m pytest 02-robot-electronics/code
```

## Exercise

> [!CAUTION]
> **Safety:** disconnect the battery — not just the switch — before touching any wiring, and check polarity with the multimeter before reconnecting ([SAFETY.md](../SAFETY.md) rule 9). Insulate the pack's leads while you work; a shorted 3S 35E pack delivers tens of amps into whatever shorted it. Wear safety glasses when clipping strands; a flying offcut travels further than you expect.

### Exercise 02.07-E1 — Size your own harness `[numerical]`

Hardware: none (a ruler is useful).

1. Measure the actual length of each power run on your robot. Update `KARMEL_RUNS` in a copy of `harness.py`.
2. Run it and record the chosen gauge, the drop and the binding constraint for each run.
3. Re-run with `--fuse 5` and with `--fuse 15`. Which rows change, and why does the fuse rating change a *wire* decision at all?
4. Suppose you upgrade to the 1:30 motors (higher stall current, same driver limit) and add a Jetson on the 5 V rail at 4 A. Which runs need a different gauge?

### Exercise 02.07-E2 — Crimp, pull, repeat `[hardware]`

Hardware: `tools` (crimper, strippers, cutters), JST XH contacts and housings, offcuts of 22 and 24 AWG.

1. Strip 2 mm of insulation. Crimp an XH contact onto AWG 22 with the correct die. Inspect: are all strands inside the conductor barrel? Is the insulation gripped by the rear wings? Is there a small bell mouth at the front?
2. **Pull test it.** Grip the wire and the contact and pull firmly. Record whether it held.
3. Make four deliberately wrong crimps and pull-test each: (a) wrong die slot (too large), (b) insulation caught in the conductor crimp, (c) only the conductor crimped, insulation wings open, (d) a crimp you then flooded with solder — then flex that one 20 times at the barrel.
4. Cut open one good and one bad crimp with side cutters and look at the cross-section.

No tools yet? Do E1 and E4, and buy the crimper before [02.08](02.08-from-breadboard-to-perfboard.md) — you will need it there anyway.

### Exercise 02.07-E3 — Build one real cable `[hardware]`

Hardware: `robot-base`, `tools`.

Replace the Dupont wiring on **one** subsystem — the sensor header is the best candidate — with a proper cable:

1. Choose the gauge and connector from your E1 table.
2. Cut to length **with a service loop**, crimp both ends, fit the housings, label both ends with the net names.
3. Anchor it within 25 mm of each connector.
4. Before connecting: beep out every pin pair with the multimeter's continuity function, and check for shorts between adjacent pins.
5. Photograph it next to the Dupont version it replaced.

### Exercise 02.07-E4 — Vibration audit `[design]`

Hardware: `robot-base` (looking at it) — no tools needed.

Go around your robot and write down, for every connector:

1. Is it keyed? Is it latching?
2. Is there an anchor within 25 mm?
3. Does anything hang from it?
4. Can any part of the cable reach a wheel, the caster or a moving part?
5. Is it labelled at both ends?

Score each connector 0–5 and rank them. Then predict which three will fail first, and write the fix for each. Keep the list — the Practical challenge is to close it.

### Exercise 02.07-E5 — Fuse coordination `[numerical]`

Hardware: none.

1. For a 10 A fuse, which of AWG 18, 20, 22 and 24 are protected by it, and what does "protected" mean here?
2. karmel's worst case is 7.57 A ([02.02](02.02-power-budget.md)). Why is the fuse 10 A and not 8 A?
3. A branch to the sensors is 24 AWG and comes off the main bus downstream of the 10 A fuse. Compute the current at which that wire is in trouble, and say what you would add.
4. What happens, physically, if a 24 AWG wire is faulted across a 3S pack with a 10 A fuse upstream? Estimate the power dissipated per metre at 10 A.

## Expected result

- **02.07-E1:** with karmel's default lengths you get AWG 20 / 20 / 20 / 22 / 28 and the binding constraints listed in the Diagram table. With `--fuse 5` the **battery run stays AWG 20** — its fuse constraint relaxes but ampacity takes over (8 A × 1.25 = 10 A needs AWG 20's 11 A) — while the driver-VIN and motor runs drop to **AWG 22** (7 A ≥ 5 A). With `--fuse 15` every fused run becomes **AWG 18**, because AWG 20's 11 A no longer covers the fuse. The fuse changes a wire decision because a fuse protects the *wire*, not the load: its whole job is to open before the wire becomes the heating element. Notice also that the binding constraint moves between rows and between fuse sizes — that is why you run the script instead of memorising a gauge. Adding a 4 A Jetson load makes the 5 V run 7.8 A worst case, which needs **AWG 18** on the drop budget alone, and the motor runs are unchanged because the DRV8874's 2.95 A limit caps them regardless of the motor.
- **02.07-E2:** a correct AWG 22 XH crimp should not move under a firm two-finger pull. Of the deliberate faults: (a) the oversized die leaves the barrel loose and the wire usually pulls straight out; (b) insulation in the conductor crimp gives a joint with high, unstable resistance that may still pass a pull test — the dangerous one, because it looks fine; (c) conductor-only crimps often survive a straight pull and fail after a few dozen flexes; (d) the soldered crimp is the **strongest in a straight pull and the first to break in flex**, usually within 20 cycles, snapping at the solder's edge. That contrast is the whole lesson.
- **02.07-E3:** continuity on every intended pair, no continuity between adjacent pins, and the cable stays put when you shake the chassis. The visual difference from the Dupont version is the point: one bundle, one connector, one anchor, two labels.
- **02.07-E4:** on a typical first build, the three worst are (1) the sensor Dupont bundle — unkeyed, unlatched, unanchored, hanging; (2) the motor-to-driver wires, if they are Dupont or bare screw-terminal strands; (3) the Pico's USB cable, which is heavy, stiff and usually unanchored. If your worst three are different, your list is better than this one — use yours.
- **02.07-E5:** (1) AWG 18 (16 A) and AWG 20 (11 A) are protected; AWG 22 (7 A) and AWG 24 (3.5 A) are not, meaning the fuse will happily pass a current that makes those wires overheat indefinitely. (2) A fuse must not open on legitimate worst-case current or you get nuisance trips during reversals; 10 A gives ≈ 32 % headroom over 7.57 A while still being far below what the pack can deliver into a short. (3) AWG 24 is in trouble above about 3.5 A, a current the 10 A fuse never notices — so add a **local fuse or a self-resetting polyfuse** (1 A is plenty for the sensor branch) at the point the branch leaves the main bus, or run the branch in AWG 20. (4) At 10 A, AWG 24 dissipates $I^2R = 100 \times 0.084 =$ **8.4 W per metre** of conductor. A 30 cm branch (60 cm of copper both ways) dissipates about 5 W in a thin PVC-insulated wire: the insulation melts within seconds, the wire glows, and the fuse never opens because 10 A is exactly what it is rated to pass. That is how wiring fires start.

## Troubleshooting

### Symptom: a connection works when you press on it

Stop using the robot and find it now; intermittent contacts destroy hours later.

1. **Wiggle test with a meter on continuity**, one connector at a time, while the battery is disconnected. The beep will stutter at the bad one.
2. If it is a Dupont contact, look into the housing from the back: a contact that has backed out is visible as a gap. Push it in until the barb clicks; if it doesn't click, the barb is flattened and the contact is scrap.
3. If it is a crimp, cut it off and redo it. Crimps are not repairable.
4. If it is a screw terminal, fit a ferrule.

### Symptom: a wire broke right at the connector

That is fatigue, and it is a strain-relief failure, not a wire failure. Redo the termination and **add the anchor** — otherwise the replacement breaks at the same place in the same number of hours. Look for the same geometry elsewhere on the robot: if one exists, more exist.

### Symptom: the motor connector gets warm

1. Measure the voltage drop *across the connector* under load, not the resistance with the power off. More than about 50 mV at 3 A (17 mΩ) means a bad contact.
2. Check the crimp's gauge against the connector's rating. A 3 A load on a 2 A PH connector runs warm by design.
3. Check for a partially inserted contact, or a housing that isn't fully mated.

### Symptom: the robot works on the bench and dies on the floor

Vibration. Do E4's audit and fix the top three. Then repeat the drive with a finger held on each suspect connector in turn, or gently tap each one with a pencil while the robot runs on a stand — a marginal contact will show up as a glitch you can reproduce on demand.

### Symptom: you can't tell which wire is which any more

You skipped Level 5. Stop, disconnect the battery, and label everything before continuing. This takes twenty minutes now and saves two hours per debugging session forever.

## Common mistakes

- **Building the whole robot with Dupont jumpers "for now".** They have no rating, no key and no latch. Fine for a breadboard, not for something that drives.
- **Sizing wire by drop only, and forgetting the fuse.** A 10 A fuse in front of 24 AWG wire is not protection, it is a heating element with a permit.
- **Forgetting the factor of 2** for the return conductor. Every drop calculation doubles.
- **Soldering crimps.** Stronger in a straight pull, dramatically weaker in flex, which is the load your robot actually applies.
- **No anchor near the connector.** All the bending then happens at the stiffest point in the assembly.
- **Letting a module hang from its wires.** Mount everything; a module on the end of a cable is a pendulum.
- **Mixing colour conventions.** A black wire that is sometimes a signal will one day be connected as a ground.
- **Cables long enough to reach a wheel.** They will.
- **Using a connector at 100 % of its rating** because the number is bigger than the current. Derate to 80 %, and use the manufacturer's rating, not the seller's.

## Knowledge check

1. Why does a 30 cm run need 60 cm of resistance in your voltage-drop calculation?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Current flows out along one conductor and back along the other. Both are in the circuit, both drop voltage, so the loop is twice the physical run. `drop_v()` multiplies by 2 for exactly this reason. Forgetting it makes every drop estimate optimistic by a factor of two.
   </details>

2. karmel's battery run needs only AWG 22 to meet its voltage-drop budget. Why does the script choose AWG 20?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Two reasons, and the drop budget is neither. Fuse coordination: the main fuse is 10 A and AWG 22's chassis-wiring rating is about 7 A, so a fault drawing 8–9 A would be passed indefinitely while cooking the wire. And ampacity with margin: the run's worst case is 8 A, and 8 × 1.25 = 10 A also exceeds 7 A. AWG 20's 11 A satisfies both.
   </details>

3. Compute the resistance of 25 cm of AWG 20, both conductors, and the drop at 3 A. Then say whether the drop or the heating constrains that run.
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   33.2 mΩ/m × 2 × 0.25 m = **16.6 mΩ**; drop = 3 × 0.0166 = **50 mV**, 0.4 % of 11.1 V — trivially inside a 3 % budget. The binding constraint is not the drop. Ampacity with the 1.25 margin rules out AWG 24 (3 × 1.25 = 3.75 A > 3.5 A), and on karmel the 10 A main fuse then rules out AWG 22 as well (7 A < 10 A) — so AWG 20, while the drop alone would have allowed AWG 26.
   </details>

4. Predict: you solder a crimp "to make it more reliable", then run the robot for a week. What happens and where?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Solder wicks up the strands past the barrel, turning a flexible stranded wire into a stiff solid one for several millimetres. All bending then concentrates at the sharp boundary where the solder stops. The copper work-hardens and cracks there, usually within tens to hundreds of flex cycles — often with the insulation intact, so the break is invisible and behaves as an intermittent contact. A plain, correctly-sized crimp with an insulation grip outlasts it by orders of magnitude.
   </details>

5. Your JST XH connector carries 3.0 A and you used AWG 24 contacts. What is wrong, and what will you observe?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   JST's 3 A rating is specified **with AWG 22**. AWG 24 has 60 % more resistance per metre and a smaller crimp cross-section, so the contact resistance is higher and the current density in the crimp is higher. Observation: the connector runs warm, the voltage drop across it grows over time as fretting oxidises the contact, and eventually it becomes an intermittent. Use AWG 22 contacts, or derate the connector.
   </details>

6. Debugging: one wheel stops intermittently on the floor and never on a stand. Where do you look, and what is the cheapest test?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   The difference between floor and stand is vibration and chassis flex, so suspect a mechanical contact failure, not the firmware. Cheapest test: run the robot on a stand and tap each connector in the motor's chain with a pencil (or wiggle each one) while watching for the glitch. That turns an intermittent into a reproducible one in a couple of minutes, and it identifies the exact connector.
   </details>

7. Why must every connector be anchored within about 25 mm, rather than just "somewhere along the cable"?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   The termination is the stiffest point in the assembly, so it is where the bending moment concentrates. An anchor close to it moves the flexing into free cable, where it is distributed over a long, compliant length. An anchor a long way down the cable leaves the near section free to whip, and the whipping is reacted at the crimp. The same geometry explains why a strain-relief boot is short and close to the connector body.
   </details>

8. You need to carry 6 A on a run and only have JST XH connectors. What do you do?
   <details><summary>Answer</summary>

   Do not use one XH way for 6 A — it is rated 3 A and you would be at 200 % even before derating. Options, in order: use an XT30 (15 A); or split the current across **multiple parallel ways** of the same XH connector (three ways with AWG 22 gives 3 × 2.4 A derated = 7.2 A, and the same for the return — this is standard practice and is why multi-way connectors carry power); or move the load so it doesn't cross a connector at all. Never assume paralleling is free: it relies on all crimps being equally good, so pull-test every one.
   </details>

## Practical challenge

Turn your robot's wiring into a **documented harness** and prove it survives.

1. Write a harness table for your robot: every run, with net name, gauge, connector, length, worst-case current, both end labels, and the anchor point. Keep it in your notes next to `karmel.yaml`.
2. Rebuild every connection that scored badly in E4: crimped, keyed, latching where it matters, labelled both ends, anchored within 25 mm, with a service loop.
3. Extend `harness.py`'s `KARMEL_RUNS` to match your robot exactly and confirm every gauge you used is at least what it chooses.
4. **Shake test:** run the robot on the floor for 20 minutes over a deliberately rough path (a rug edge, a tile seam, a threshold strip) while logging `bus_v` and encoder counts. Then repeat the E4 audit.

**Acceptance criteria:** a harness table that a stranger could use to rebuild the robot; zero unlatched connectors in any run carrying more than 100 mA; every connector anchored within 25 mm with a photo showing it; `harness.py` agreeing with every gauge you used; and a 20-minute rough-surface run with no dropouts, no glitches in the logs, and nothing loose in the post-run audit.

## You can skip this if…

You answer knowledge-check questions 2, 4, 5 and 7 correctly without looking, and your robot's wiring already uses keyed, latching connectors with correct-gauge crimps, strain relief within 25 mm, and labels at both ends.

## Go deeper

- JST, XH connector series: https://www.jst-mfg.com/product/detail_e.php?series=277 — the source of the 3 A / AWG 22 / 250 V rating; the PDF drawing gives the contact dimensions the crimper die must match.
- JST, PH connector series: https://www.jst-mfg.com/product/detail_e.php?series=199 — 2 A / AWG 24 / 100 V; this is the family your Yahboom motor's encoder cable uses.
- Holybro, Connector & Wire Rating: https://docs.holybro.com/power-module-and-pdb/power-module/connector-and-wire-rating — the clearest citable XT60 numbers (30 A continuous, 60 A burst with 12 AWG).
- PowerStream, Wire gauge and current limits: https://www.powerstream.com/Wire_Size.htm — the chassis-wiring and resistance tables `harness.py` compares itself against.
- NASA-STD-8739.4, Crimping, Interconnecting Cables, Harnesses, and Wiring: https://standards.nasa.gov/standard/NASA/NASA-STD-87394 — the definitive description of what a correct crimp looks like, with photographs of every defect; skim the crimp inspection section.
- SparkFun, Working with Wire: https://learn.sparkfun.com/tutorials/working-with-wire — stripping, gauges and basic termination, with pictures.
- [FE.04 Breadboards and connectors](../optional-foundations/electronics/FE.04-breadboards-and-connectors.md) and [FE.17 Soldering](../optional-foundations/electronics/FE.17-soldering.md) — the foundation lessons this one assumes.
